notes:
I found good verse-by-verse material from Enduring Word, Bible Hub (Ellicott, Pulpit, Gill, Geneva, Matthew Henry and others), Bible.org (Deffinbaugh and Utley), StudyLight, TGC, Precept Austin, Bible Odyssey and Catholic Answers. The one verse where traditions clearly split is Onan's sin (vv. 8–10). I didn't find anything from netbible.org, the Orthodox sites (oca.org, newadvent.org), the Pentecostal or Lutheran sites themselves, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so those are left out.

---

## Part 1: Verse-by-verse notes (traditional reading)

**Chapter as a whole**
- Ellicott says the chapter isn't a break in the story. It shows how close the family came to being absorbed by the Canaanites, and it belongs to the Messiah's family tree. the first, that it shows the great risk of utter contamination incurred by the patriarchs in living among the Canaanites; the second, and more important, that Judah was invested by his father with the rights of primogeniture — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Deffinbaugh (Bible.org) says the chapter explains why the move to Egypt was needed, and sets up a contrast with Joseph's purity in chapter 39. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 1**
- Ellicott thinks "at that time" can't mean the moment Joseph was sold, because 22 years isn't long enough for everything in the chapter. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Ellicott places Adullam in the Elah valley. Judah "went down" because the road drops from the hill country to the lowland. — same URL
- Guzik notes that Judah was Leah's fourth son and was the one who suggested selling Joseph (Gen 37:26). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Deffinbaugh calls Hirah a bad influence: wherever Hirah shows up, Judah is in trouble. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 2**
- Guzik calls this an ungodly and unwise marriage to a Canaanite woman, noting that the patriarchs had discouraged such marriages. — https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Gen/Gen_38.cfm
- Deffinbaugh points out that "saw… took… went in to" closely echoes Shechem taking Dinah (34:2). He suggests the choice was based on looks alone. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- Ellicott: the Targum reads "Canaanite" as "merchant," but he doubts the two words meant the same thing that early. Shua is the woman's father, not her own name. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm

**vv. 3–5**
- Ellicott links Chezib with Achzib near Adullam (Micah 1:14–15). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Gaebelein reads the names as symbols: Er = "enmity," Onan = "wickedness," Shelah = "the sprout," a picture of a future godly remnant. His offspring is Er (enmity) and Onan (wickedness) till the significant third one comes, Shelah (the sprout) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/genesis-38.html

**v. 6**
- Utley: Tamar means "palm tree." Choosing the son's wife was the father's role in that culture. — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38
- Guzik: since Judah had a Canaanite wife himself, it's no surprise he chose a Canaanite for Er. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Pulpit Commentary (citing Lange): Judah may have married his sons young to stop corruption taking root in them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Guzik: we aren't told what Er's sin was, but it was serious enough to bring immediate judgment. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Pulpit Commentary notes the wordplay between Er (עֵר) and "evil" (רַע). It suggests the sin may have been "some unnatural abomination," and that God may have let Er's own indulgence lead to an early death. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: levirate marriage is much older than Moses' law. The Mosaic Law did not institute, but regulated the custom. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Guzik: the custom kept the dead brother's name alive and gave the widow children to support her. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Deffinbaugh: the Mosaic Law often confirmed customs that already existed. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: Onan may have wanted the firstborn's rights for his own line. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: the Hebrew means "whenever," so it happened repeatedly. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-9.htm
- Constable says the same: this was his persistent practice. When (9) should be translated 'whenever.' — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/38-9.html
- Gill: the child would have counted as Er's son and inherited his estate. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-9.htm
- (For the debate over what exactly the sin was, see Part 2.)

**v. 10**
- Gill: God was displeased because of Onan's envy and greed, and because it hindered Abraham's seed and the line the Messiah would come from. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-10.htm
- Constable: Onan was working against God's promises to the patriarchs. — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/38-9.html

**v. 11**
- Commentators disagree about Judah's motive:
  - One commentator on Bible Hub says Judah evidently believes that the deaths of Er and Onan are somehow due to Tamar and uses Shelah's age as an excuse. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-11.htm
  - Ellicott says it doesn't follow that he blamed her; losing two sons would scare anyone. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
  - TGC agrees with the first view: Judah blamed Tamar instead of seeing that his sons were the problem. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/judah-in-the-gospel-of-jesus/
- Geneva note: Tamar couldn't marry into another family while Judah kept her attached to his. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-11.htm
- Guzik: Tamar was not at fault; the blame belonged to Judah and his sons. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: Timnah is probably the town on the Philistine border (Tibneh). The Septuagint and Vulgate read "his shepherd Hirah" instead of "his friend." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Deffinbaugh: losing his wife left Judah vulnerable in a sexually loose society. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 13**
- TGC: Sheep-shearing was party time, much like Mardi Gras is today. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/judah-in-the-gospel-of-jesus/
- Deffinbaugh makes the same point about the mood of sheep-shearing season. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "Enaim" means "two fountains." It was apparently the town where Tamar's father lived. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Guzik: Tamar couldn't find a husband on her own. Judah, as her head, had to give her one. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Utley: veils were uncommon before Islamic times (compare Rebekah in 24:65). Taking off her widow's clothes shows she still felt tied to Judah's family. — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: Jewish commentators agree that harlots didn't usually veil. Judah may have taken her for a woman fulfilling a vow to Astarte, so the kid goat would have been a sacrifice to the goddess. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Ellicott also reports Lange's view that Er, like Onan, had neglected Tamar, so there was "no real incest." — same URL

**v. 16**
- Deffinbaugh: Judah bargained like an experienced man, so this was probably not his first time with a prostitute. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 17**
- Deffinbaugh: asking for a pledge was probably normal, since a customer couldn't be made to pay afterward. Tamar wasn't interested in payment. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: Judah probably wore his seal on a cord around his neck. Staffs were decorated, and kings' sceptres developed from them. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Deffinbaugh: a cylinder seal was unique to its owner and worked like an ID card. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- Utley: Tamar planned in detail and wanted these items as proof of who the father was. — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38
- Guzik: the conception wasn't Judah's intention, but it was Tamar's plan more importantly, it was in God's plan. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/

**v. 19**
- Utley: Tamar immediately went home which shows that prostitution was not her purpose or lifestyle! — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38

**vv. 20–22**
- Ellicott: Hirah used the word *kedeshah*, "one consecrated," and "Enaim by the wayside" seems to have been the village's full name. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Bible.org (Deffinbaugh's footnote, quoting a source): *qedesah* means a religious prostitute linked to fertility-goddess shrines. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: Maimonides argued Judah broke no law. Ellicott replies that Judah plainly saw his act as shameful and would rather lose his seal and staff than be exposed. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: legally Tamar counted as Shelah's wife, so Judah, as head of the family, gave the usual sentence for adultery. Jewish commentators guessed she came from a priestly family; some linked her to Melchizedek. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Deffinbaugh: because she was pledged to Shelah, this was adultery, not just fornication. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- Guzik: Judah found it easy to condemn someone else for the sin he had committed himself. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/

**v. 25**
- Utley: the verb "examine/recognize" is the same one used in 37:32–33, when the brothers asked Jacob to "examine" Joseph's coat. — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38
- Ellicott: the Talmud praises Tamar for not shaming Judah in public. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Guzik: she made the logical point that the man who hired her was just as guilty. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/

**v. 26**
- Pulpit Commentary: Tamar was far from innocent, but she was less guilty than Judah. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-26.htm
- One older commentator on the same page says she was more unchaste because she knowingly committed incest, but he was more unjust because he caused her sin. — same URL
- Gill: "more righteous" refers to how they dealt with each other, not the sexual sin itself. — same URL
- Several commentators on that page take "he did not know her again" as proof that his confession was sincere. — same URL
- The Bible Hub chapter summary links this confession to Judah's later change, when he pleads for Benjamin (Gen 44). — https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/genesis/38.htm
- TGC: Judah declared her innocence and admitted his own guilt. Tamar was more faithful to the standards of her culture—in pursuing the levirate custom—than he was to his. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/judah-in-the-gospel-of-jesus/

**v. 27**
- Deffinbaugh: the first twin to emerge got the firstborn's rights, which is why a mark was needed. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30

**v. 28**
- Gill: the hard birth may have been a correction for her sin. The thread was tied on to identify the firstborn. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-28.htm
- The Bible Hub summary sees the scarlet thread as pointing ahead to the Passover blood and Christ's blood. — https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/genesis/38.htm

**v. 29**
- Perez means "breach." The Geneva note says Their heinous sin was signified by this monstrous birth. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-29.htm
- TGC: the younger son winning out over the older recalls Jacob and Esau. — https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/judah-in-the-gospel-of-jesus/

**v. 30**
- Ellicott: Zerah means "rising" (as of the sun), probably a nod to the red thread. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
- Guzik: Perez is in Jesus' family line (Matt 1:3; Luke 3:33), This is a wonderful example of grace. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Matthew Henry: the chapter shows that God's choice is of grace and not of merit. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-11.htm

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 8–10: What was Onan's sin?**
- **Reformers and older Protestants (Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist, Anglican):** These quotes come from a Catholic site quoting Charles Provan's collection, not from each tradition's own websites.
  - It quotes Luther calling the act a "sodomitic sin" and Calvin calling it killing a son before he is born. — https://www.catholic.com/tract/birth-control and https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/calvins-contraception-contradiction
  - It quotes Wesley warning that "thousands, especially of single persons" still displease the Lord this way. — https://www.catholic.com/tract/birth-control
  - It quotes Anglican archbishop James Ussher and Puritan Cotton Mather on the same lines. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/protestants-against-contraception
- **Gill (Baptist):** the sin, named "Onania" after Onan, is condemned by nature and by God's word. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-9.htm
- **Today's evangelical consensus:** Onan's sin was a selfish refusal of his duty, not masturbation or birth control.
  - GotQuestions: the sin of Onan was his greedy, selfish refusal to sire a son on behalf of his brother. — https://www.gotquestions.org/onanism.html
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) agrees: it wasn't masturbation, but a refusal to care for the widow and a selfish use of sex. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
  - A Bible.org Q&A says the same. — https://bible.org/question/what-does-bible-say-about-birth-control
- **A middle view (Deffinbaugh, Bible.org):** Onan was condemned for three things: an act against nature, disobedience, and selfish motives. But this passage alone doesn't make all birth control sinful, because we haven't been commanded to raise up offspring the way he was. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- **Coffman (Church of Christ):** strongly rejects the Catholic reading. The sin was selfish greed and fraud against Tamar. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/genesis-38.html

**vv. 14–26: How should Tamar be judged?** Opinions range from heroine to sinner:
- Utley says it was not an act of lust, but, in my opinion, an act of religious faith and calls her the real heroine. — https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-38
- Deffinbaugh: Judah was wrong, but so was Tamar for taking matters into her own hands. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- Guzik: she was treated unjustly but used immorality to get her way. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-38/
- Gaebelein calls her sin "dark and vile." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/genesis-38.html
- A sermon quoted on Precept Austin even says she blackmailed Judah for revenge. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-1-commentary

## Part 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- Pulpit Commentary reports that critics (Tuch, Bleek, Colenso and others) called the chapter a later "Jehovistic" insertion. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/38-1.htm
- Deffinbaugh pushes back against liberal scholars who treat the chapter as an interruption. — https://bible.org/seriespage/38-skeleton-judah-s-closet-genesis-381-30
- Bible Odyssey:
  - Tamar was probably Canaanite, though the text doesn't say. — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/people/related-articles/tamar-genesis/
  - The problem is solved by Tamar herself, not by Judah or Shelah. — same URL
  - Her name means "date palm." — https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/tamar/

**Catholic**
- Catholic Answers holds that The Lord took Onan's life because Onan engaged in contraceptive sex, which goes against the natural order. — https://www.catholic.com/qa/onan-up-to-contraceptive-sin
- Their argument: the Law's penalty for refusing levirate duty was public shame, not death, so Onan's sin must have been more than refusing the duty. — https://www.catholic.com/tract/birth-control
- They admit that in recent years both Protestant and Catholic commentators have downplayed this reading. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-sin-of-onan
- One Catholic writer grants that the passage, taken alone, only addresses this one form of contraception. — https://www.catholic.com/magazine/blog/onan-died-for-this-and-nothing-else
- Pius XI's *Casti Connubii* is cited as reading the passage this way. — https://www.catholic.com/video/is-nfp-just-catholic-birth-control

**Jewish tradition (as reported by Ellicott)**
- Philippsohn says a widow who had lost two husbands came to be called *Katlannith*, "the murderess." Ellicott notes Matthew 22:25–26 shows no such rule. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/38.htm
